title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Preface
Somewhere on your hard drive there is a folder with a paper in it, and in that folder there is a file called figure1.pdf.
Where did it come from? Which script made it? Was that script the current version of the script, or the one from before you fixed the bug in the data-generating function? If a reviewer asks you to change the sample sizes from 50, 100 and 400 to 50, 100, 400 and 1000, how many things do you have to remember to rerun, and in what order, before the number in the abstract is right again?
Most of us answer these questions with memory and discipline. Both work fine until the project gets big, or a coauthor touches it, or you come back to it after eight months. This tutorial is about answering them with a file instead.
A workflow manager is a program that you tell, once, which files depend on which other files and what command turns one into the other. After that it will build anything you ask for, run only what is actually out of date, and refuse to let a figure in your manuscript be older than the code that made it (unless you explicitly override it which isn’t easy to do). This tutorial focuses on one particular workflow manager: Snakemake.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Who this is for
Statisticians and biostatisticians who write R, run simulations, and produce manuscripts or analysis reports. You should be comfortable in R. You do not need to know Python (Snakemake is written in Python, and its files are Python, but you will need about five minutes’ worth of it, all of which is explained), and you do not need to have used make or any other build tool.
Everything here runs on a laptop. However, one of Snakemake’s (many) party tricks is that the same workflow can be dispatched to a cluster by adding a configuration file and changing nothing else, but that is out of scope; Where to go next points at where to read about it when you need it.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
What we build
One example runs through most of the book. It is a small simulation study of a problem every biostatistician has been asked about: what happens to confidence intervals when the model was chosen using the same data.
In this example we will: generate data, select variables by forward selection, and compare the intervals you get by naively refitting against the intervals you get by splitting the sample. Then we compute this over a grid of sample sizes and correlation levels, turn the results into a figure and a table, and compile the whole thing into a manuscript — so that changing one line of the simulation code and typing snakemake rebuilds the PDF, correctly, every time.
By the end the pipeline looks like this:





flowchart LR
  C[code/sim.R] --> S1[18 simulation<br/>result files]
  S1 --> F[out/figure1.pdf]
  S1 --> T[out/table1.tex]
  F --> P[build/paper.pdf]
  T --> P
  M[main.tex] --> P
  M --> R[build/submission.pdf]
  F --> R
  T --> R






8  A data analysis pipeline then applies the same ideas to a piece of applied collaborative work — raw CSV, cleaning, models, Table 1, rendered report — for readers whose focus is analysis rather than methods research (most of us). I focus on the manuscript pipeline here because it parallels where I learned Snakemake, in my dissertation work.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Installing Snakemake
Snakemake is a Python package. Once you have a Python setup you like, install it there. E.g.:
python3 -m pip install snakemake
Check that it worked:
snakemake --version
This “book” was written against Snakemake 9.13. Version 8 introduced a number of changes to how cluster execution is configured, and a few flags used here do not exist in version 7 or earlier.
You will also want R with optparse and ggplot2; 7  Building the manuscript additionally uses tidyr, kableExtra and a LaTeX installation, and 8  A data analysis pipeline uses knitr and Quarto. Each example’s README.md lists what it needs.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Getting the examples
Every code block in this book is printed from a file in the examples/ directory of the tutorial repository, and every terminal transcript is pasted from a real run of that code. Nothing here is pseudocode. Clone the repository and follow along:
git clone https://github.com/lharris421/snakemake-tutorial.git
cd snakemake-tutorial/examples/01-first-rules
snakemake --cores 2

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Acknowledgments
The format and spirit of this tutorial are modeled on the University of Iowa Biostatistics HPC tutorial by Patrick Breheny and Grant Brown, whose final chapter on Snakemake is the seed this grew from. The manuscript structure in 7  Building the manuscript follows the conventions in Patrick Breheny’s manuscript template.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.1 Interactive work is not reproducible
Snakemake does not run R code. It runs commands, and it decides when to run them. So before any of it is useful, your analysis has to be something you can start from a terminal without clicking anything — and, ideally, something you can point at different parameter values without editing the file.
This chapter has nothing to do with Snakemake. If you already write scripts that take arguments and save their output to a file you name, skip to Chapter 2.
It is worth being blunt about this once, because everything else in the book follows from it.
Whatever is in your R session right now is the product of a history nobody has, including you. Objects created by code you have since edited or deleted. A package loaded by hand in March. A seed set before an experiment you abandoned. And if you saved the workspace on exit, all of that invisible state came back with you the next morning.
The practical consequence is that “it works” is not a claim you can check. A number in your session may or may not be what the current version of your code produces. There is no way to find out except to start a clean session and run the code from the top — which is exactly what running a script does.
None of this is an argument against working interactively. Interactive is how you figure out what the code should be; it is the right tool for exploring a dataset, staring at a model, and getting a plot to look right. The rule is narrower than that: nothing may exist only in your session. Once a piece of analysis is real, it belongs in a file that runs top to bottom, in a fresh session, and writes its output somewhere you named.
Snakemake is the machinery that makes the rule livable: it reruns from a clean session only the parts that are actually out of date, so insisting on scripts stops costing you the thing interactive work was buying.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
TipDon’t save your workspace



Turn off the .RData prompt — in RStudio, Tools → Global Options → General, set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never and clear “Restore .RData into workspace at startup”. Per project, the same two settings are SaveWorkspace: No and RestoreWorkspace: No in the .Rproj file; this repository’s has both.
It feels like losing something. What you lose is the illusion that your results survive a restart, and finding that out early is much cheaper than finding it out the week a paper is due.
crumbs: 1  Running R from the command line

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.2 Rscript
Rscript runs an R file top to bottom and exits:
Rscript sim.R
Two things change when your code runs this way rather than in RStudio.
The first is that the working directory is wherever your terminal is, not wherever the file is. If sim.R says readRDS("rds/thing.rds"), that path is resolved relative to the directory you were sitting in when you typed the command. Pick a convention and hold to it; the one used throughout this book is always run from the project root, so every path in every script is relative to the top of the project. Snakemake follows the same convention by default, which is convenient.
The second is that nothing prints unless you ask. Auto-printing at the top level is an interactive feature, so head(d) on its own line produces no output under Rscript; you need print(head(d)) or cat(). This matters more than it sounds like it should, because those prints become your log file in Chapter 5.
crumbs: 1  Running R from the command line

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.3 Taking arguments
A script that hard-codes n <- 100 can only ever do one thing. To run the same code at three sample sizes you would have to edit the file between runs, which is exactly the kind of manual step we are trying to eliminate. Instead, read the values from the command line.
The base R way is commandArgs(), which hands you the arguments as a character vector:


sim.R (excerpt)

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
method <- args[1]
outfile <- args[2]

and is then called like this:
Rscript sim.R naive rds/sim-naive.rds
This is fine for two arguments. It gets bad quickly: the arguments are positional, so you have to remember the order, everything arrives as a character string that you have to convert yourself, and there is no way to give something a default.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.4 optparse
The optparse package gives you named flags with types and defaults, which is what the rest of this book uses:


sim.R (excerpt)

library(optparse)

option_list <- list(
  make_option("--n", type = "integer", default = 100),
  make_option("--rho", type = "integer", default = 50),   # as a percent
  make_option("--method", type = "character", default = "naive"),
  make_option("--iterations", type = "integer", default = 200),
  make_option("--seed", type = "double", default = 1234),
  make_option("--out", type = "character", default = "rds/sim.rds")
)
opt <- parse_args(OptionParser(option_list = option_list))

Now the script is called with named arguments in any order:
Rscript sim.R --n 400 --rho 80 --method split --out rds/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds
and opt is a list: opt$n is an integer, opt$method is a string. Anything you leave off falls back to its default, so the script still runs as-is when you are poking at it interactively.






TipDefaults are documentation



Set the defaults to the values you use most often. Someone reading make_option("--iterations", type = "integer", default = 200) learns both what the flag is called and what a normal value looks like, and you get a script that runs unmodified when you source it by hand.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.5 One script, one output file
The last convention, and the one Snakemake actually requires: a script should write to a path it was told, not a path it invented.


sim.R (excerpt)

dir.create(dirname(opt$out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(res, opt$out)
cat("wrote", opt$out, "-- coverage:", round(mean(res$covered), 3), "\n")

Note the dir.create(). Snakemake creates the directories for a rule’s declared outputs before running it, but scripts that also work when you run them by hand shouldn’t count on that.
This is what makes a script composable. sim.R does not know it is part of a pipeline; it knows how to turn a set of parameters into one file. The Snakefile in the next chapter is nothing more than a list of which parameters go with which filename.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.6 Where the results go
Two decisions that will save you pain later:
Results are files, and files are named for what produced them. A file called n400_rho80_split.rds tells you the sample size, the correlation, and the method. A file called results2_final.rds tells you nothing, and in six months neither will you.
Git is for source, not output. Commit the scripts and the inputs; let everything the code produces be rebuilt. That covers figures and tables as firmly as it covers a 200 MB .rds file — a figure is output no matter how small it is.
Computed results and finished products live in separate directories. Every example in this book writes serialized results — the expensive part — to rds/, and figures and tables to out/. Nothing is written anywhere else, and neither directory is tracked. It draws a clean line between the things that took an afternoon to compute and the things that can be redrawn in a second. Section 2.8 says more about the layout once you have seen a Snakefile.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.1 Rules
Start in examples/01-first-rules. It contains two R scripts — sim.R, which runs the simulation for one method, and figure.R, which turns simulation output into a figure — and a file called Snakefile.
By hand, building the figure means running three commands in the right order:
That is not hard. It is just something you have to remember, and remember again every time you change one of the scripts, and remember correctly — because nothing stops you from rebuilding the figure without rerunning the simulation.
A Snakefile is a list of rules. A rule says: here are the files I need, here is the file I produce, and here is the command that gets from one to the other.
Read rule sim_naive as a sentence: to make rds/sim-naive.rds, given sim.R, run Rscript sim.R naive rds/sim-naive.rds.
A few mechanics:

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
Snakefile

rule all:
    input:
        "out/figure1.pdf"

rule sim_naive:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim-naive.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R naive {output}"

rule sim_split:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim-split.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R split {output}"

rule figure:
    input:
        script = "figure.R",
        rds = ["rds/sim-naive.rds", "rds/sim-split.rds"]
    output:
        "out/figure1.pdf"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} {output} {input.rds}"




{output} and {input} are substituted into the shell command. You write the filename once, in the output: block, and refer to it after that. This is not just brevity — it makes it impossible for the rule to declare one file and write a different one.
Inputs can be named, as in rule figure, where input.script and input.rds are referred to separately in the command. Without names, {input} expands to all of them, space-separated, in order.
Indentation matters, as in Python. Use four spaces and stay consistent.
sim.R is listed as an input, even though it is code rather than data. This is important. It is what makes “the script changed” a reason to rerun.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.2 rule all
rule all is different. It has no output and no command — only inputs. It exists because of a rule Snakemake follows strictly:

Snakemake builds the first rule in the file, and whatever that rule needs.

So rule all is where you list the things you actually want to exist at the end. Everything else gets built because something in that list, directly or indirectly, depends on it. A file that is not reachable from rule all will not be built, no matter how many rules could make it. By convention this is named rule all, but what matters is that it is first.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.3 The dependency graph
From those four rules Snakemake works out the order for itself. Nothing in the file says the simulations come before the figure; it deduces that from the fact that rule figure needs files that rule sim_naive and rule sim_split produce.





flowchart LR
  A[sim.R] --> B[rds/sim-naive.rds]
  A --> C[rds/sim-split.rds]
  D[figure.R] --> E[out/figure1.pdf]
  B --> E
  C --> E
  E --> F([rule all])






This is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Two consequences worth internalizing early: anything with no path between the nodes can run at the same time (Chapter 5), and a cycle is an error rather than an infinite loop (it won’t run).

title: 2  A first Snakefile
section: 2.6 What counts as out of date
text:
2.6 What counts as out of date
Here is where Snakemake differs from make, and from most people’s expectations.
make asks one question: is the input newer than the output? If so, rebuild.
Snakemake asks two, and needs both answers to be yes. It keeps a record of every output it has ever made — in a directory called .snakemake/ — including a SHA-256 checksum of each input that went into it. A job is out of date when

an input’s timestamp is newer than the output’s, and
that input’s contents differ from what was recorded.

The timestamp is the gate and the checksum is the confirmation. So:
$ touch code/sim.R && snakemake -n
Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).
Touching a file does not trigger a rebuild, because the contents did not change. Change one character of sim.R, though, and everything downstream of it goes:
$ echo '## a real edit' >> code/sim.R && snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        2
sim              18
table1            1
total            23
(That transcript comes from the larger example of Chapter 7, which is why there are 23 jobs rather than 4.)
Content is not the only trigger. Snakemake also stores the shell command and the parameters used for each output, so editing a rule’s command — not just the script it calls — makes the affected outputs stale too. Chapter 9 covers how to inspect and override all of this.






WarningThe timestamp really is a gate



Because the check is an and, a changed file whose timestamp is not newer than the output is invisible: Snakemake never gets as far as comparing the checksum. You will not produce that situation by editing a file — editing sets the timestamp to now — but you can arrive at it by other routes, because several common tools preserve timestamps deliberately:
cp -p old/sim.R code/sim.R      # -p preserves the original mtime
rsync -a backup/ .              # -a implies -t
tar xf archive.tar              # restores the archived mtimes
Restore a script from a backup or an archive that way and the pipeline can sit there insisting everything is up to date. If you have moved files around by any means other than editing them, touch the ones you restored, or force the issue with snakemake -R (Chapter 9).








NoteDeleting .snakemake/ is safe



It is a cache of metadata, not results. Delete it and the next run rebuilds everything, because Snakemake no longer has any record of how the existing files were made. Add it to .gitignore and otherwise ignore it.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.7 Building one thing
You can also name a target directly, which is invaluable when you are developing and want to check one piece:
snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim-naive.rds
Snakemake finds the rule that can produce that file, builds whatever it needs, and stops. You can also name a rule — snakemake --cores 1 figure — which asks for that rule’s outputs.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.8 One Snakefile, one project
Before going further, it is worth being explicit about what a “project” is here, because every example in this book is one and your own work should be too.
examples/01-first-rules is a complete, self-contained project. Copy that directory anywhere on your disk and everything still works — it has no dependency on the rest of this repository. The same is true of each of the other four. They are laid out side by side for convenience, but each is a miniature of a real repository: one paper, one analysis, one thing.
The layout that scales from these examples up to a real methods paper is:


the shape of a project

my-project/
  Snakefile          <- the map: every rule, in one file, at the root
  config.yaml        <- the settings (chapter 4)
  code/              <- the scripts the rules call
  rds/               <- computed results
  out/               <- figures and tables

Three of those deserve to be stated as rules rather than suggestions.
One Snakefile, at the root. Not one per subdirectory. The Snakefile is the only place that describes how the pieces of the project fit together, so a newcomer — a coauthor, a reviewer, you in a year — has exactly one file to open to find out what this project builds and what it builds it from. Snakemake does let you split rules across files with include:, and that is worth reaching for once a single file becomes genuinely unwieldy, but the default should be one file you can read top to bottom.
rds/ holds what the pipeline computes. Simulation output, fitted models, cleaned data — the objects that took time to produce and that everything else is derived from. They are serialized R objects, hence the name; use whatever name you like, but use one directory.
out/ holds what a human looks at. Figures and tables: the things that end up in the manuscript or the report.
The reason to split these rather than pile everything into one results/ folder is that the two halves behave completely differently. rds/ is expensive, is reused across a paper and a talk and a grant renewal, and may take days to regenerate — it is the thing worth backing up and worth sending to a coauthor. out/ is cheap: delete it and snakemake puts it back in seconds, from the contents of rds/. Once they are separate directories you can treat them differently, and Chapter 10 does exactly that.
The corollary is that anything not in rds/ or out/ is either code, settings, or something a human wrote. That is a useful thing to be able to say about a directory — and it is what makes the next rule easy to apply.
Neither rds/ nor out/ is tracked by git. Not because they are large, or binary, or likely to go stale — those are consequences, and reasoning from them means relitigating the question for every new kind of file. The rule is simpler than that:

Git is for source, not output.

Source is what a person wrote: the scripts, the Snakefile, the config, the .tex files. Everything in rds/ and out/ was produced by running that source, so none of it belongs in the repository.


.gitignore

rds/
out/
.snakemake/

Stated that way it also settles the case people otherwise talk themselves out of. A figure is small and it is genuinely convenient to look at a PDF on GitHub — but size has nothing to do with whether something is source, and out/figure1.pdf is as much an output as a four hundred megabyte .rds. If you want to see the figures, run snakemake. It takes seconds, and what you get is guaranteed to match the code you are looking at.
The one thing this costs you is that a fresh clone cannot show anybody a result until it has been rebuilt. When the rebuild takes days rather than seconds that is a real cost, and Chapter 10 deals with it — by sharing rds/ outside of git, not by committing it.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.9 Try it

Delete out/ and rebuild. Time it. Then delete rds/ as well and compare.
Change the n <- 100 line in sim.R to n <- 200 and run snakemake -n. Which jobs are planned, and why?
Add a line to rule all asking for out/nonexistent.pdf and run snakemake -n. Read the error carefully — you will see it again.

title: 3  One rule, many jobs
text:
3.1 A wildcard is a hole in a filename
Look again at the Snakefile from the last chapter and notice how much of it is copied and pasted:
Two rules, identical but for the word naive versus split. Now imagine the real version of this simulation: three sample sizes, three correlation levels, two methods. Eighteen rules, all the same, and one typo away from a figure that silently mixes up two scenarios.
Wildcards fix this. Move to examples/02-wildcards.
The output is no longer a filename; it is a pattern. The parts in braces are wildcards, and they work backwards: when something asks for rds/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds, Snakemake matches that name against the pattern, concludes that n is 400, rho is 80 and method is split, and substitutes those values into the command wherever {wildcards.…} appears.
This is the mental adjustment that makes Snakemake click. You do not tell it to run the simulation eighteen times. You tell it what a result file is called as a function of its parameters, and then you ask for the files you want.

title: 3  One rule, many jobs
text:
Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--out {output}"









ImportantWildcards match anything, including nonsense



A wildcard is a regular expression, .+ by default. Nothing in the rule above says method has to be naive or split, so asking for rds/sim/n50_rho0_bayes.rds produces a perfectly valid job that runs sim.R --method bayes and fails inside R. Chapter 4 shows how to constrain wildcards, and Chapter 9 shows what that failure looks like.

title: 3  One rule, many jobs
text:
3.2 Naming files so this works
Wildcards make your file-naming scheme part of the pipeline’s logic, which is worth two minutes of thought up front:

Put every parameter that changes into the name. If two runs differ in anything, their outputs must differ in name, or one will overwrite the other and Snakemake will believe both are up to date.
Use a separator that cannot appear in a value. These examples use _ between fields and stick to digits and lowercase letters within a field.
Keep it parseable in the other direction too. You will eventually want to read n400_rho80_split.rds back into columns in R.

The scheme here is n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds, with rho as a percentage so that it stays an integer — rho50 rather than rho0.5, because a decimal point in a filename is an invitation to trouble.

title: 3  One rule, many jobs
text:
3.3 expand()
Something still has to say which eighteen files we want. That is expand():


Snakefile (excerpt)

N = [50, 100, 400]
RHO = [0, 50, 80]
METHODS = ["naive", "split"]



Snakefile (excerpt)

rule figure:
    input:
        script = "figure.R",
        rds = expand("rds/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds",
                     n=N, rho=RHO, method=METHODS)
    output:
        "out/figure1.pdf"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} {output} {input.rds}"

expand() takes a pattern and some lists and returns every combination of them, so
expand("rds/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds", n=N, rho=RHO, method=METHODS)
returns a list of 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 filenames. Those are the inputs of rule figure, which is what causes all eighteen simulations to run.






NoteThe Python you need



N = [50, 100, 400] is a list, the same idea as c(50, 100, 400) in R. That is essentially the entire Python vocabulary required to use Snakemake: lists, strings in quotes, and the occasional dictionary in Chapter 4.


Note that expand() fills wildcards in, and {wildcards.n} reads them back out. These are opposite operations, and it is worth being clear about which one you are doing: expand() appears in the rule that consumes many files, and {wildcards.…} in the rule that produces one.

3.5 Building one cell of the grid
Because the output is a pattern, you can ask for any file it can match, whether or not anything else wants it:
$ snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
Using shell: /bin/bash
Provided cores: 1 (use --cores to define parallelism)
Rules claiming more threads will be scaled down.
Job stats:

-----  -------
sim          1
total        1

Select jobs to execute...
Execute 1 jobs...

localrule sim:
    input: sim.R
    output: rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
    jobid: 0
    reason: Missing output files: rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
    wildcards: n=50, rho=0, method=naive
    resources: tmpdir=/var/folders/gz/hbrw64n97wb0vy5prhnxst400000gp/T
wrote rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds -- coverage: 0.823 

Finished jobid: 0 (Rule: sim)

This is how you develop. Rather than running the whole grid to find out whether your new method works, ask for one small scenario, look at it, and only then let the rest go.
This is also extremely powerful, because now if you want a certain simulation… you just ahve to ask for it rather than edit an R file and run it.

title: 4  Configuration
text:
4.1 config.yaml
sim.R in Chapter 3 has 200 iterations written into it, which is the wrong place: you will want 20 while you are debugging and 1000 for the final results, and changing that should not mean editing the simulation code.
Move to examples/03-config, which puts all of it in one file.
YAML is about as simple as it looks: key: value, one per line, lists in square brackets, # for comments. Load it at the top of the Snakefile:
and everything in it is available as config, a dictionary: config["iterations"] is 200. Use config.get("key", default) when a setting is optional.
Notice how little is in there. A config is for settings that apply to the project as a whole — iterations means the same thing to every rule that computes anything.

title: 4  Configuration
text:
config.yaml

# Settings that apply to the whole project.  Drop `iterations` to 20 for a fast
# run that checks the plumbing; put it back to 200 for results you would show
# anyone.
iterations: 200




Snakefile (excerpt)

configfile: "config.yaml"

title: 4  Configuration
section: 4.2 Runs that don’t overwrite each other
text:
4.2 Runs that don’t overwrite each other
This one setting is treated differently, and it is the most useful idea in this chapter. iterations is not passed to the script and forgotten — it names the directory the results go in:


Snakefile (excerpt)

## The iteration count names the directory the results go in, so a 20-iteration
## smoke run and a 1000-iteration final run sit side by side instead of
## overwriting each other.  ITER picks which of them the figure is built from.
ITER = config["iterations"]



Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        script = "code/sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--iterations {wildcards.iterations} "
        "--out {output}"

{ITER} never appears in that rule: the count arrives as the wildcard {wildcards.iterations}, read back out of the filename that was asked for by rule figure, just like {wildcards.n}.
The figure rule collects the set ITER points at:


Snakefile (excerpt)

        rds = expand("rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds",
                     iterations = ITER,
                     n = [50, 100, 400],
                     rho = [0, 50, 80],
                     method = ["naive", "split"])

title: 4  Configuration
text:
4.3 wildcard_constraints
Chapter 3 warned that a wildcard matches anything. Constraints fix that:


Snakefile (excerpt)

wildcard_constraints:
    iterations = r"\d+",
    n = r"\d+",
    rho = r"\d+",
    method = "[a-z]+"

r"\d+" is a regular expression matching one or more digits; the r prefix marks a raw string, so the backslash reaches the regex intact. Declared at the top level they apply to every rule, and they can also be attached to a single rule, as Chapter 7 does.
Two reasons to bother:
Ambiguity. With unconstrained wildcards there is more than one way to match n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds against a name containing extra underscores, and Snakemake resolves it by its rules rather than yours.
Failing early. Without the \d+ on {n}, asking for rds/200/sim/nfifty_rho0_naive.rds matches quite happily —
wildcards: iterations=200, n=fifty, rho=0, method=naive
— and Snakemake goes off and runs sim.R --n fifty, which dies inside R however long the job takes to get that far. With the constraint, nothing can produce that file and you are told so before anything starts.
A misspelled extension is a different matter: n50_rho0_naive.RDS fails whether or not you have constraints, because the pattern ends in a literal .rds and .RDS is not that. Constraints police the wildcards, not the text around them.

title: 4  Configuration
text:
4.4 Overriding from the command line
Any config value can be replaced for a single run with --config:
snakemake --cores 4 --config iterations=20
which is the fastest way to check that a pipeline is wired up before committing to the real thing:
$ snakemake --cores 4 --config iterations=20

real    0m3.683s
user    0m4.825s
sys 0m0.636s
$ snakemake --cores 4

real    0m9.937s
user    0m27.534s
sys 0m0.798s
Five seconds against eleven, for a grid that would take considerably longer at the iteration counts of a real paper.






Warning--config does not always rebuild what you expect



What an override actually rebuilds depends on how the setting is used, and the two cases here behave differently:

--config iterations=20 asks for different files. Eighteen new simulations run; the old ones are left alone.
Dropping a sample size from a rule’s expand() is a Snakefile edit rather than a config one, and it reruns no simulations at all — the remaining results are still perfectly valid. The figure does rerun, with the reason Set of input files has changed since last execution, because it is now summarizing twelve files instead of eighteen.

Note that --config wants one key=value per setting and will not take a list on the command line (--config n=[50,100] is a parse error on 9.13). Change the grid in config.yaml, or point --configfile at a second YAML file whose values override the first.
When you want to force the issue, snakemake --forcerun sim reruns every job of that rule regardless. See Chapter 9.

title: 4  Configuration
text:
4.5 Where to draw the line
A useful test: if changing it changes the results, it belongs in the config; if changing it changes what the code does, it belongs in the code.
Iteration counts and file locations — config. The definition of the estimator — code. The temptation, once you have a config file, is to make everything configurable, and you end up with a 200-line YAML file harder to read than the code it configures. The config here has one setting, and it is the one that genuinely applies to everything.

title: 4  Configuration
text:
4.6 Try it

Run with --config iterations=20, then again with --config iterations=200. What does Snakemake rerun, and why?
Add 1000 to the n list in config.yaml and run snakemake -n.
Delete the wildcard_constraints block and ask for rds/sim/n50_rho0_na_ive.rds. What happens, and what did {method} match?

title: 5  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
5.1 –cores
Once your work is expressed as a DAG, you get the parallelism for free — Snakemake already knows which jobs do not depend on each other.
With eighteen independent simulations and four cores, four run, and as each finishes another starts, until all eighteen are done and the figure can go. There is nothing to configure — the ordering falls out of the DAG.
--cores all uses every core you have. On a laptop you are also using for other things, leave one or two free; on a shared server, be a good citizen and pick a reasonable number.

title: 5  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
snakemake --cores 4








NoteTwo kinds of parallel



--cores controls how many jobs run at once, and that is usually the only kind of parallelism you need for a simulation study. It is unrelated to parallelism inside a job (mclapply, future, a multithreaded BLAS). If a rule does use threads internally, tell Snakemake with threads: so its accounting stays honest:
rule sim:
    threads: 4
    shell: "Rscript sim.R --cores {threads} ..."
Then --cores 8 runs two such jobs at a time rather than eight.

title: 5  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
5.2 Logs
Once eighteen jobs are interleaving their output, the terminal becomes unreadable, and the run you actually want to look at scrolled past an hour ago. The log: directive gives each job its own file:


Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        script = "code/sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    log:
        "logs/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.log"
    benchmark:
        "benchmarks/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.tsv"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--iterations {wildcards.iterations} "
        "--out {output} > {log} 2>&1"

Two details. The log file is declared by log: but nothing writes to it automatically — the redirection > {log} 2>&1 at the end of the shell command is what does it (2>&1 catches errors as well as normal output). And the log path carries the same wildcards as the output, so each job gets its own file rather than eighteen jobs overwriting one.
Anything the script prints lands there:
$ cat logs/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.log
wrote rds/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.rds -- coverage: 0.78 
Which is worth designing for. A script that prints its parameters, its sample size after exclusions, and a summary of what it computed gives you a log directory that answers most questions without rerunning anything. Chapter 8 leans on this heavily.
Logs also survive failure. When a job dies, Snakemake tells you which log to read, and the R error message is sitting in it — as opposed to being lost in the scrollback of a parallel run.






ImportantSnakemake will not delete a log file



Outputs of a failed job are removed so that a half-written file is never mistaken for a real one. Logs are deliberately kept, because they are the evidence. This also means a log from a successful run sticks around until the job runs again.

title: 5  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
5.3 Benchmarks
benchmark: records how long a job took:
rule sim:
    benchmark: "benchmarks/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.tsv"
$ cat benchmarks/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.tsv
s   h:m:s   max_rss max_vms max_uss max_pss io_in   io_out  mean_load   cpu_time
1.59    0:00:01 0   0   0   0   0.00    0.00    64.69   0
The first column is seconds. This is how you find out that one corner of your parameter grid takes forty times as long as the rest, which is worth knowing before you scale the whole grid up by a factor of ten.

title: 5  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
5.4 Interrupting and resuming
Snakemake is designed to handle being stopped.
Terminating processes on user request, this might take some time.
What survives is everything that had already finished. Those outputs stay on disk, and the next run does not rebuild them; it starts from wherever the interruption left the pipeline. So the cost of stopping a twelve-hour run after four hours is only the handful of jobs that were in flight at that moment.
The jobs that were in flight need one more thought, because a killed job may have got as far as writing part of its output. Snakemake tracks that, and rather than letting a truncated file pass for a real result it stops the next run:
IncompleteFilesException:
The files below seem to be incomplete. …
Incomplete files:
rds/200/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds
The fix is to say so explicitly:
snakemake --cores 4 --rerun-incomplete
which discards the suspect files and rebuilds them.

text:
5.5 Try it

In examples/03-config, run with --cores 1, then --cores 4, and compare. Why is the speedup less than four?
Delete one simulation’s .rds file and run again. How many jobs run?
Add a log: directive to the figure rule in examples/03-config and check that ggsave’s output ends up in it.

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
6.1 The aggregating rule
Everything so far has produced .rds files, which nobody reads. This chapter turns them into the two things a paper is actually made of. Move to examples/04-manuscript, which is the complete version of the simulation study.
A figure rule looks like any other rule; what distinguishes it is that its input is the whole grid rather than one cell:
The expand() sits in the rule that needs it. rule table1 next to it writes out the same call, because it happens to summarize the same grid — but it is free not to, and a supplementary figure covering only the large sample sizes would simply sweep less.
The R script receives all eighteen filenames as trailing arguments and stacks them:
positional_arguments = TRUE tells optparse to accept bare arguments alongside the named flags, so the script can be called as
An alternative worth knowing about: instead of passing filenames, the script could glob rds/200/sim/ itself. Do not do this. A glob picks up whatever happens to be lying in the directory, including results from a parameter grid you abandoned last month, and it hides the dependency from Snakemake, which will then happily build your figure without running the simulations.

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
Snakefile (excerpt)

rule figure1:
    input:
        script = "code/figure.R",
        rds = expand("rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds",
                     iterations = ITER,
                     n = [50, 100, 400],
                     rho = [0, 50, 80],
                     method = ["naive", "split"])
    output:
        "out/figure1.pdf"
    log:
        "logs/figure1.log"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} --out {output} "
        "{input.rds} > {log} 2>&1"





code/figure.R (excerpt)

parsed <- parse_args(OptionParser(option_list = option_list),
                     positional_arguments = TRUE)
opt <- parsed$options
infiles <- parsed$args

res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(infiles, readRDS))


Rscript code/figure.R --out out/figure1.pdf rds/200/sim/*.rds

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
6.2 Figures
Nothing about the plotting code is Snakemake-specific — it is the ggsave() call you would write anyway:


code/figure.R (excerpt)

p <- ggplot(cov, aes(n, covered, color = method, group = method)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = opt$level, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~rho) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sort(unique(cov$n))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors, labels = method_labels) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "n", y = sprintf("Coverage of %g%% CI", 100 * opt$level),
       color = "Method") +
  theme_minimal()

dir.create(dirname(opt$out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
ggsave(opt$out, p, width = 7, height = 3)
cat("wrote", opt$out, "\n")

Two conventions, though, that matter more inside a pipeline than outside one:
Write vector graphics to the size they will appear. ggsave(..., width = 7, height = 3) in inches, matching the text width of the document, means the figure is never rescaled by LaTeX and the fonts in it come out the size you chose. Resizing a figure by 60% in \includegraphics is how you end up with axis labels nobody can read.
Name the methods once, at the top of the script. The figure and the table both turn naive into something a reader sees:


code/figure.R (excerpt)

method_labels <- c(
  "naive" = "Naive",
  "split" = "Sample splitting"
)

colors <- c("naive" = "#d95f02", "split" = "#1b9e77")

so that the spelling and the color are decided in one visible place rather than buried in a ggplot call.






NoteShared code belongs in files of its own



Each script here is short enough to read top to bottom, so everything it needs sits at the top of it. A real project outgrows that quickly, in two directions.
Values used by more than one script — the labels and colors above, a plotting theme, the levels of a factor — go in a small script the others source, something like code/setup.R. Defining them once is what stops a figure and the table beside it disagreeing about what naive is called.
Functions get a directory, with one function per file. Put them in R/, each file named for the function it defines: R/gen_data.R, R/select_forward.R, R/eval_cis.R. Finding the function you want a year from now is then a matter of reading the file listing.
The reason for that particular directory name is that it is what an R package uses, and the distance between a directory of functions and a package is two lines:


DESCRIPTION

Package: mymethods
Version: 0.0.1

With that file present, devtools::load_all() loads everything in R/ in one call, and the project is on its way to being installable and citable without a line of code moving. The methods repository in Chapter 10 has sixteen files in R/, organized exactly this way.
Whichever you are doing, there is one Snakemake-specific thing to remember: list what a script sources as an input to the rules that call it.
rule sim:
    input:
        script = "code/sim.R",
        functions = ["R/gen_data.R", "R/select_forward.R"]
Without those lines the dependency is invisible, and editing a function leaves every result that used it silently stale — the one failure mode Snakemake cannot warn you about (Chapter 9). A shortcut once R/ has more than a handful of files: functions = glob.glob("R/*.R") catches the lot, at the cost of rerunning everything whenever any of them changes.
When the functions are the contribution rather than the scaffolding, that package in waiting should become a real one, which is where Chapter 10 picks the story up.

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
6.3 Tables
Tables are the same idea with a different output format: the script writes a LaTeX fragment that the manuscript \inputs.


code/table.R (excerpt)

## escape = FALSE so that "$n$" reaches LaTeX as math rather than as literal
## dollar signs; the price is that anything else in the table must be valid LaTeX
tab <- kbl(wide, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, linesep = "",
           escape = FALSE,
           col.names = c("$n$", rep(unname(method_labels), 2)),
           align = c("r", rep("c", ncol(wide) - 1)),
           caption = sprintf(paste("Coverage of nominal %g\\%% confidence",
             "intervals for coefficients selected by forward selection, by",
             "whether the selected coefficient is truly zero."),
             100 * opt$level),
           label = "coverage") |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Non-null" = 2, "Null" = 2))

which produces:


out/table1.tex

\begin{table}

\caption{\label{tab:coverage}Coverage of nominal 95\% confidence intervals for coefficients selected by forward selection, by whether the selected coefficient is truly zero.}
\centering
\begin{tabular}[t]{rcccc}
\toprule
\multicolumn{1}{c}{ } & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Non-null} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Null} \\
\cmidrule(l{3pt}r{3pt}){2-3} \cmidrule(l{3pt}r{3pt}){4-5}
$n$ & Naive & Sample splitting & Naive & Sample splitting\\
\midrule
50 & 0.917 & 0.941 & 0.598 & 0.952\\
100 & 0.944 & 0.957 & 0.619 & 0.928\\
400 & 0.939 & 0.943 & 0.564 & 0.944\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Points worth noting:

The file contains a fragment, not a document — no \documentclass, no \begin{document}. It is meant to be \input into something else.
The caption and label live with the numbers, not in the manuscript. That way \ref{tab:coverage} resolves and the caption cannot describe a table that the code no longer produces.
escape = FALSE lets $n$ through as math. The cost is that everything else in the table must then be valid LaTeX — a % or _ in a variable name will break the build, which is a reasonable trade when you control the contents.

Writing .tex rather than pasting numbers into the manuscript by hand is the entire argument of this book, applied to tables. A number in your paper should be traceable to the code that computed it, and the only way to guarantee that is for no human hand to touch it in between.

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
6.4 rule all as the manifest
With figures and tables in place, rule all becomes the list of everything the paper is made of:


Snakefile (excerpt)

rule all:
    input:
        "build/paper.pdf",
        "build/submission.pdf"

Here it names only the two PDFs, because everything else is reachable through them. In a larger project — the one in Chapter 10 has sixteen figures and tables — it is common to list every product explicitly instead:
rule all:
    input:
        "build/paper.pdf",
        "out/figure1.pdf",
        "out/figure2.pdf",
        ...
This is slightly redundant, and it is what you want anyway. It gives you one place to read off what the project produces, and it means snakemake still builds a figure you have temporarily commented out of the manuscript while you rearrange the results section.

title: 6  Figures and tables
text:
6.5 Try it

Change the color palette in code/figure.R and run snakemake -n. Does the table rebuild? Should it?
Add a figure2 rule showing coverage against rho instead of n, and add it to rule all.
Delete out/table1.tex and run snakemake --cores 4. How far back does Snakemake go?

title: 7  Building the manuscript
text:
7.1 The rule
Here is the situation this chapter is about. You are using an editor that rebuilds your PDF every time you save, so the document always matches its LaTeX source. It does not match its figures: out/figure1.pdf was made by some script at some point, and if you change the simulation nothing tells the manuscript about it. The document is only as current as the last time you remembered to rerun things.
Making the manuscript a rule closes that gap.
latexmk is doing the LaTeX-specific work — running pdflatex and BibTeX as many times as it takes for references and citations to settle. Snakemake’s contribution is the input: block: the PDF depends on the figure and the table, which depend on the simulations, which depend on the code. One command now walks the entire chain.
The wildcard {doc} builds either document with the same rule, constrained to the two names that exist. wildcard_constraints is attached to this rule rather than declared at the top of the file, since it is only meaningful here.

title: 7  Building the manuscript
text:
Snakefile (excerpt)

## The manuscript depends on the figure and the table, which depend on the
## simulations, which depend on the code.  That chain is the whole point: change
## sim.R and `snakemake` rebuilds the PDF, through every step in between.
rule manuscript:
    input:
        tex = "{doc}.tex",
        shared = ["main.tex", "preamble.tex"],
        config = "config.yaml",
        figure = "out/figure1.pdf",
        table = "out/table1.tex"
    output:
        "build/{doc}.pdf"
    log:
        "logs/{doc}-latexmk.log"
    wildcard_constraints:
        doc = "paper|submission"
    shell:
        "latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -outdir=build {input.tex} "
        "> {log} 2>&1"

title: 7  Building the manuscript
7  Building the manuscript
text:
7.3 The cascade
This is the payoff, so it is worth watching happen. Everything is currently built and up to date. Now change one line in the simulation code:
$ echo '## a real edit' >> code/sim.R && snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        2
sim              18
table1            1
total            23
Twenty-three jobs: eighteen simulations, the figure, the table, and both PDFs. In the right order, with no decisions from you, and — the part that matters — with no possibility of a version of the paper containing a figure from before the change.
Compare the alternative, which is remembering to run four things in order and being right about it every time, for the entire life of the project.

title: 7  Building the manuscript
text:
7.4 Making LaTeX quiet
Two flags in that rule are there for the sake of your terminal:
-interaction=nonstopmode stops LaTeX from halting at an error to ask you what to do. In a pipeline, an interactive prompt is a hang, not a question.
> {log} 2>&1 sends the several hundred lines LaTeX produces to logs/paper-latexmk.log. When the build fails, the error is in there, and latexmk also leaves the more readable build/paper.log.






WarningLaTeX’s own idea of what is up to date



latexmk does its own dependency tracking and will sometimes decide there is nothing to do even when Snakemake has just asked it to rebuild. If a rerun leaves the PDF unchanged when you expected otherwise, delete the build/ directory and try again — and note that this is exactly why the compiled PDF should not be the only place a result appears.

title: 7  Building the manuscript
text:
7.5 What goes in git
The .gitignore for a project of this shape:


.gitignore

.snakemake/
rds/
out/
logs/
benchmarks/
build/

Same rule as Section 2.8 — git is for source, not output — which puts the compiled PDF on the ignored side of the line along with everything else. It is produced by running latexmk, so it is output, however much it feels like the point of the project. Commit the code, the .tex files, and config.yaml; the claim that the rest is regenerable is now enforced by a program rather than by your recollection.
The awkward case is a simulation that takes three days, which colleagues who clone the repository cannot rebuild over coffee. The answer is still not to commit it. Send them rds/, or keep it somewhere outside the repository that the Snakefile knows how to find; either way it travels beside the repository rather than inside it. This is the payoff for keeping rds/ separate from out/ — you hand over the expensive half on its own, and every figure, table and PDF rebuilds from it in seconds. Chapter 10 covers the mechanics.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.1 The pipeline
Most biostatisticians spend more time on analyses than on simulation studies, and the shape of the work is different: instead of a fan-out over a parameter grid, a mostly linear chain from a file someone emailed you to a report you send back. The Snakemake ideas transfer directly, and one of them — the report as a rule — addresses a problem specific to this kind of work.
Move to examples/05-analysis. It is a small randomized trial: 200 participants, two arms, FEV1 measured at baseline and week 12.
flowchart LR
  R[data/trial.csv] --> C[rds/analysis.rds]
  C --> M[rds/models.rds]
  C --> T[rds/table1.rds]
  C --> F[out/figure1.png]
  M --> P[report.html]
  T --> P
  F --> P
  C --> P

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
$ snakemake --cores 4
Job stats:
job        count
-------  -------
all            1
clean          1
figure1        1
model          1
report         1
table1         1
total          6

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.2 Raw data is read-only
The first rule reads data/trial.csv and never writes to it. That is not a Snakemake requirement; it is the convention that makes everything else work, and it deserves stating plainly: the raw file stays exactly as it arrived. Every correction, exclusion and recoding happens in code, downstream, where it can be read and argued with.
Note also what is not in the Snakefile. data/make-raw-data.R, which generated the CSV for this example, is not a rule. If it were, Snakemake would treat the raw data as something it could regenerate, and would do so — silently discarding the real file the moment it decided it was out of date. Anything you cannot afford to lose should be an input to your pipeline and never an output of it.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.3 Cleaning once


code/clean.R (excerpt)

raw <- read.csv(opt$infile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
log_step <- function(d, msg) {
  cat(sprintf("%-45s n = %d\n", msg, nrow(d)))
  invisible(d)
}
log_step(raw, "raw file")

d <- raw[!duplicated(raw$patient_id), ]
log_step(d, "after dropping duplicate patient records")

## Sex arrives as F/f/female/Female/M/male/Male
d$sex <- ifelse(toupper(substr(d$sex, 1, 1)) == "F", "Female", "Male")

## Ages over 120 are data entry errors, not centenarians
d$age[d$age > 120] <- NA
log_step(d[!is.na(d$age), ], "with a usable age")

d$visit_date <- as.Date(d$visit_date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
d$arm <- factor(d$arm, levels = arm_levels)
d$smoker <- factor(d$smoker, levels = c("Never", "Former", "Current"))
d$change <- d$fev1_wk12 - d$fev1_base

## The primary analysis needs a week 12 measurement
d <- d[!is.na(d$change), ]
log_step(d, "with a week 12 measurement (analysis set)")

Every decision about the data is in this one script, and it announces each one:
$ cat logs/clean.log
raw file                                      n = 201
after dropping duplicate patient records      n = 200
with a usable age                             n = 199
with a week 12 measurement (analysis set)     n = 191
wrote rds/analysis.rds 
That is the participant flow for your CONSORT diagram, produced as a side effect of the pipeline rather than counted by hand, and regenerated every time the data changes. When the coordinator sends an updated export in June, snakemake reruns everything downstream and this log tells you immediately whether the exclusions still look the way they did in March.
The alternative — each analysis script starting with its own read.csv() and its own quiet decisions about who to drop — is how two tables in the same report end up with different denominators.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
section: 8.4 The report is a view, not a computation
text:
8.4 The report is a view, not a computation
Here is the part specific to analysis work. It is normal to put everything in one .qmd file: read the data, fit the models, print the tables, write the text. It works, and it has two failure modes that get worse as the project grows.
The first is time. A report that refits everything takes as long as the slowest model every time you fix a typo, and the temptation is to start caching chunks, at which point you no longer know whether the numbers in the output correspond to the code in the file.
The second is scope. Rendering becomes all-or-nothing — you cannot ask for just the models — and the results exist only inside the rendered HTML, so the next project that needs them starts by copying and pasting.
Splitting it fixes both. The scripts compute and save; the report reads and displays:


report.qmd (excerpt)

```{r}
#| include: false
library(knitr)
analysis <- readRDS("rds/analysis.rds")
tab1 <- readRDS("rds/table1.rds")
models <- readRDS("rds/models.rds")
eff <- models$effects
```

The report does no computing of its own. It reads the objects the pipeline
produced and displays them, so that rendering it can never quietly change a
result.



Snakefile (excerpt)

## Listing every object the report reads is what makes the report trustworthy:
## it cannot be rendered against a stale table or a figure from last month.
rule report:
    input:
        qmd = "report.qmd",
        analysis = "rds/analysis.rds",
        models = "rds/models.rds",
        table1 = "rds/table1.rds",
        figure1 = "out/figure1.png"
    output:
        "report.html"
    log:
        "logs/report.log"
    shell:
        "quarto render {input.qmd} --to html > {log} 2>&1"

Listing each object the report reads is what makes the report trustworthy. Rendering it cannot use a stale table, because Snakemake will rebuild the table first. And the models are in rds/models.rds, so the manuscript you write next year can load them without rerunning anything.
Everything the report needs to say in prose comes through inline R:


report.qmd (excerpt)

The estimated treatment effect is
`r sprintf("%.3f L (95%% CI %.3f to %.3f)", eff$estimate[eff$model == "adjusted"], eff$lower[eff$model == "adjusted"], eff$upper[eff$model == "adjusted"])`
in the adjusted model, and is insensitive to which covariates are included.

so the sentence and the table cannot disagree.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.5 Models as data


code/model.R (excerpt)

specs <- list(
  unadjusted = change ~ arm,
  adjusted   = change ~ arm + age + sex + fev1_base,
  full       = change ~ arm + age + sex + bmi + smoker + fev1_base
)

fits <- lapply(specs, function(f) lm(f, data = d))

## Pull the treatment effect out of each fit into one tidy data frame
effects <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
  fit <- fits[[nm]]
  ci <- confint(fit)["armTreatment", ]
  data.frame(model = nm,
             estimate = unname(coef(fit)["armTreatment"]),
             lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
             p = summary(fit)$coefficients["armTreatment", "Pr(>|t|)"],
             n = length(residuals(fit)),
             row.names = NULL)
}))

Two things worth copying here. The model specifications are a named list, so adding a sensitivity analysis means adding one line and touching nothing else. And the script saves both the fitted objects and a tidy data frame of the estimand — the first for anything you did not anticipate, the second so the report does not need to know how to dig a confidence interval out of an lm.
$ cat logs/model.log
       model estimate  lower upper        p   n
1 unadjusted    0.161 0.0876 0.234 2.41e-05 191
2   adjusted    0.162 0.0875 0.236 2.79e-05 190
3       full    0.176 0.0994 0.252 1.01e-05 178
wrote rds/models.rds

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.6 When the data changes
Which it will, usually the week after you send the report. Drop in the new export and:
snakemake --cores 4
Cleaning reruns, the models refit, Table 1 and the figure regenerate, the report re-renders, and the participant-flow log tells you what changed about the analysis set. The work of a data update goes from an afternoon of retracing your steps to one command and a careful look at one log file.
